transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. ___. What brings you in today?

Um, hi. My mom actually made the appointment and drove me here because... well, she's been getting really worried, or maybe frustrated, I don't know. It's just... mostly I just can't make myself do anything anymore. I don't really know how else to explain it. It's like my battery is completely empty. I just sit in my room all day long. I'm actually wearing the exact same clothes I've had on for days, I haven't even changed to sleep, I just stay in them. I just sit on the edge of my bed. 

I used to do a lot of things, you know? Like, I used to knit, I had all these half-finished scarves and a big basket of yarn, and I used to write in my journal every single night without fail, and I'd go for long walks around the neighborhood just to get fresh air... but now, the thought of doing any of that is just... I can't. I look at the yarn and I can't even make my hands pick it up. And my mom will come into my room and she'll stand there asking me what's wrong, over and over, asking why I'm just sitting there, why I won't do anything... and I hear her, but I barely even have the energy to answer her. It takes so much effort just to open my mouth and make a sound, so I usually just don't. I just let her talk. I guess that's why she brought me to see you.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

Um... depressed? No. No, I don't think so. I know that's what my mom thinks is happening, because she's always coming into my room and asking if I'm sad, or she'll ask if I've been crying while she was out at the grocery store, but I haven't been. Sad is... well, sad is like a real feeling, you know? Like, when I was a sophomore in high school and my grandfather died, I was so sad, I cried for like a week straight and my chest actually physically ached. 

But this isn't like that at all. I don't feel sad or down or miserable. It's more like... I just don't feel much of anything. It's completely flat. I'll sit there on the edge of the bed looking at the wall or the carpet, and I'm not having these dark, heavy thoughts, I'm just kind of... existing. The hours just go by and I don't really feel them. So I definitely wouldn't say I feel depressed. It's just that everything is sort of scooped out. There's no sadness, because there's just nothing really there to be sad with. My mom keeps trying to bring me my favorite snacks or she'll suggest we watch a funny movie in the living room to cheer me up, but you can't really cheer up someone who isn't actually sad in the first place, you know? I try to tell her I'm not crying, but she just looks at me like I'm hiding it. But I'm really not.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Um... I don't know if "lost interest" is really the right way to describe it. Because it's not like I suddenly hate knitting or think it's stupid now. I still have this one really soft, chunky blue yarn sitting right on my nightstand, it's the kind of yarn that's really thick and warm, and I know I like it. I know it's a good color, I picked it out specifically at the craft store a while ago. And my journal, it has this nice leather cover with a little strap, and I know I usually like writing in it with this specific black gel pen because the ink glides really smoothly over the paper... I know those are things I enjoy. Or, well, things I know are enjoyable. 

But when I look at them now, I don't have this thought of, 'ugh, I don't care about this anymore' or 'this is pointless.' I just... don't feel the spark to reach out and grab them. It's not a loss of liking it, it's just... I don't know. Like with the snacks my mom brings. She brought me those little cheddar cheese crackers yesterday, the ones shaped like little squares that I've eaten since I was like, seven years old. I know they taste good. I know I like them. But I just let the bowl sit there on the blanket next to me until they got stale because the whole process of picking one up, chewing it, tasting it... it just didn't happen. 

So I don't think I lost interest, not really. The interest is still there in the room, I guess, I just can't connect to it. Does that make sense? Because my mom keeps saying I must hate my hobbies now since I won't touch them, and I have to keep explaining to her—well, in my head I explain it, because like I said, talking takes too much energy—that I don't hate them, I'm just sitting there instead.
Have you ever had a period of at least four days when you felt unusually high, irritable, or full of energy?

Um, high? Like, full of energy? No. Definitely not. I mean, like I was trying to explain earlier, my battery is just totally empty, so having too much energy is pretty much the exact opposite of what I experience. I don't think I've ever had a time where I felt like I had extra energy to burn. Even back in high school, before I just started sitting in my room all the time, I was always just kind of a normal, quiet person. I never had days where I was bouncing off the walls or feeling like I could take on the world or anything like that. 

And irritable... I mean, my mom gets frustrated with me, like I mentioned, when she stands in my doorway and asks me questions over and over, but I don't get mad at her. I don't snap at her or feel irritable at all. I just sit there. Because, if you think about it, anger or irritability is a really active feeling, you know? You have to have fuel to burn to be mad, your heart has to race and you have to want to push back, and I just don't have any fuel for that. It takes way too much effort to be angry. 

It's funny, because sometimes I actually think my mom almost wishes I would get mad, or get super energetic, just so I'd be doing something, literally anything other than just staring at the carpet in the same clothes. Like, if I suddenly jumped up and decided to clean the whole house or knit ten scarves in a row, she'd probably be thrilled, but that's just never happened. I've never had four days like that. I don't think I've even had four minutes like that. So, no, definitely no extra energy or feeling high.
Has this low-energy, emotionally flat state been going on most days for at least two years?

Um... two years? Yeah. Actually, it's been a little longer than that. This whole decline, or whatever you want to call it, has been going on since I started the community-college program. That was about two years and two months ago. 

I know the exact timeline because it was the fall right after I graduated high school, and my mom was so excited for me to start taking classes. We went to the campus bookstore together and got my textbooks, and we bought these color-coded folders, and I had this whole class schedule printed out and taped to the back of my bedroom door. I was supposed to take an intro to history class and some English composition class, I think. But... I only went for maybe a week or two before this whole flat feeling just really took over completely. 

I remember sitting in the lecture hall for history and just staring at the back of the plastic chair in front of me, just kind of tracing the little scratches in the plastic with my eyes, and realizing I just didn't have the energy to lift my pen or even process what the professor was saying. The battery was just gone. And then I just stopped going. I started staying in my room, just sitting on the edge of the bed looking at the carpet, exactly like I do now. 

So, yeah, it’s been going on most days—really, pretty much every single day—since that semester started two years and two months ago. The days just sort of blur together into one long, flat line since then, because when you're just existing, a Tuesday feels exactly the same as a Saturday. My mom still hasn't taken that printed schedule off my door, actually. I look at it sometimes when I'm sitting there. It's just hanging there, curling at the bottom edges where the tape is giving out, but I don't have the energy to peel it off, and I guess she doesn't want to either. So it's definitely been over two years of this.
Even though you’ve said you don’t feel sad, have there been times over these past two years when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

Um... depressed or down? No, not really. Because, like I was trying to explain with the hobbies and the energy, feeling down still feels like it requires some kind of emotional weight, you know? Like, if you're depressed, I imagine you feel heavy or sad or you cry, or you have these dark thoughts circling in your head. But I don't have any of that. It's just... blank. It's not a heavy feeling, it's just an empty feeling. 

I actually remember my mom asking me something similar, maybe a year ago? It was winter, I know because I was wearing this thick gray sweater she bought me, the one with the big buttons down the front, and I was just sitting on my bed staring at the corner of the room where the paint is peeling a little bit. And she came in and sat next to me and she was crying, and she asked, "Are you so sad, honey? Are you just so depressed you can't move?" And I remember looking at her and trying to find some sadness in myself to match hers, because she was so upset, but there was just nothing there. I didn't feel like crying. I didn't feel sorrow. I didn't feel anything at all. 

So I told her no, I'm not sad. And I think that almost confused her more. Because people expect that if you're not doing anything, if you're just existing in your room for two years, you must be drowning in this deep, dark depression. But I'm not drowning. It's more like... the water just evaporated. There's no water to drown in. There's no sadness, no feeling down. Just the flat line. So, no, I haven't had times where I felt depressed most of the day, because I don't really feel much of anything most of the day.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when, aside from the flatness, you felt so depressed or down that it seriously interfered with your ability to function?

Um, no, I haven't. I mean, I know you just asked about feeling depressed or down, and I guess this is kind of the same thing, but for two weeks? No. Not even for two weeks. Like I was saying, there's just no water to drown in. It's not like I have this baseline of being flat and then suddenly, for a couple of weeks, I dip down into this really dark, heavy depression where I can't function because I'm so sad. 

My functioning is already... well, it's already what it is. I sit in my room. I look at the carpet. But it's not because I'm overwhelmed by sadness or despair. It's just the emptiness. I don't have these episodes where the flatness suddenly turns into some intense, agonizing depression that stops me from doing things. The flatness is what stops me from doing things. 

I remember reading once, back when I used to read things for that English class I never finished, about how depression can make people feel like they're walking through molasses, you know? Like everything is thick and heavy and takes so much effort just to push through. But for me, it's not like walking through molasses. It's like... not walking at all. It's like the concept of walking just doesn't even apply anymore. There's no struggle against a heavy feeling, there's just an absence of the drive to move. 

So, no, I haven't had any two-week periods where I felt so depressed it interfered with my functioning. My functioning has been exactly the same—just sitting there, staring at the floor, listening to the hum of the refrigerator from the kitchen—every day for the last two years and two months. There hasn't been any dip into sadness or anything like that. Just the same flat line, day after day, week after week.
Have you ever had any period of at least two weeks when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

Um, no. I mean, I know you're asking about the two weeks thing again, but it's really just exactly like I was saying before. There hasn't been a time where I felt depressed or down like that. Not for two weeks, not for two days. It's just... I think people really struggle to understand that you can be completely non-functional without being sad. 

Like, my mom, she's always trying to find a reason for it. She'll come into my room and she'll open the curtains, the ones with the little blue flowers on them that we picked out when I was in middle school, and she'll say, "Let some light in, maybe it'll lift your mood." And the light comes in, and it hits the carpet, and I can see all the little dust motes floating in the sunbeam, just drifting around in the air. I can watch them for hours, just seeing how they catch the light and then disappear into the shadows near the closet door. But watching them doesn't make me feel better, and it doesn't make me feel worse. It just... is. 

I don't have a mood to lift. That's the thing. If I was depressed, like really down and sad for two weeks, maybe the sunlight would hurt my eyes, or maybe I'd want to hide under the covers and cry because the world is too bright and I'm too sad. But I don't do that. I just sit there on the edge of the bed and look at the dust motes. I don't feel the urge to cry, I don't feel a heaviness in my chest. I just feel the complete absence of anything. 

So, no, there's never been a two-week period of feeling clearly depressed or down. It's always just the flat line. The same flat line since I started that community college program two years and two months ago. Just me, the carpet, the dust motes, and the tape curling on the back of my door. No sadness. Just... blank.
Have you ever had a time that lasted at least two weeks when, in addition to this flat feeling, you also lost your appetite?

Um... lost my appetite? No. No, I haven't. I mean, it's just like the other things we were talking about. It's not like I get excited about food, but I haven't lost my appetite, not for two weeks or even a few days. 

My mom, she brings me meals on this little wooden tray. It has these handles cut into the sides, and the varnish is kind of wearing off on the left corner where she always grips it. She brings it in three times a day, like clockwork. Sometimes she makes those little frozen pizza rolls, or sometimes it's just a turkey sandwich, and she actually cuts the crusts off now, which she hasn't done since I was maybe seven years old. I think she does it because she thinks I'm fragile now, or maybe she just wants to feel like she's doing something special to take care of me since I don't leave the room. 

But I eat it. I don't look at the tray and feel sick, or think, "Oh, I can't possibly eat." I just take the plate, and I sit on the edge of the bed, and I chew. I'll take a bite of the sandwich, and I'll chew it, and I'll swallow it, and then I'll take a sip of water from the blue plastic cup she always brings. It's just mechanics, you know? Like putting gas in a car that's just sitting in the driveway and never going anywhere. 

Sometimes I'll sit there for an hour, just holding a piece of bread, looking at the way the crust is slightly darker on one side, feeling the soft texture of it between my fingers before I take the next bite. I can feel the crumbs falling onto the blanket. But I always finish it. It doesn't really taste like much anymore—not good, not bad, just texture and chewing. But my stomach still growls if she's late bringing the tray. Like, if she goes to the grocery store and lunch is at two instead of noon, my stomach makes noises. My body still knows it needs food, even if my brain doesn't really care about eating. 

So, no, there hasn't been any time where I stopped eating or lost my appetite like that. I just eat the food she brings in the exact same flat way I do everything else. I just sit there, and I chew, and I watch the crumbs fall.
Have you ever had any two-week period in your life when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

Um, didn't you... I'm pretty sure you just asked me that exact same question a few minutes ago. About the two weeks and feeling depressed most of the day? I know you probably have a list of things you have to ask, or boxes you need to check off on your clipboard, but the answer is still exactly the same as it was before. No. I haven't ever had two weeks like that. 

It's strange, though, how time works when you're just... sitting. Two weeks sounds like a really specific, long amount of time when you say it like that, but for me, two weeks is just fourteen days of watching the ceiling fan. We have this ceiling fan in my bedroom, it has four blades, and one of them is slightly warped. It droops down just a fraction of an inch more than the other three. The blades are wood-paneled on one side and plain white on the other, and my dad installed it white-side down when I was ten because he said it made the ceiling look higher. 

I just lie on the bed and watch it not spinning. I can trace the dust along the edge of the warped blade with my eyes. Sometimes I think about what it would feel like to actually care that it's warped, or to feel sad that fourteen days—or a whole month, or a year—are just slipping by while I look at it. If I were actually depressed, like really down the way you keep asking about, maybe I'd cry about wasting my time or something. People who are depressed feel heavy and miserable about things like that, right? They feel bad about themselves. But I don't feel miserable. I don't feel anything about the fan, or the two weeks, or the fact that it's been over a year since high school ended and I'm just here in this room. 

So, yeah, no. I haven't been depressed or down for two weeks. There's no sadness to it. It's just the flat. Just the warped fan blade, and the quiet, and the flat.
Have you been feeling worthless or like a failure?

Um, worthless? Or a failure? No... I don't think so. I mean, to feel like a failure, you have to actually have a goal that you care about failing at, right? You have to feel some kind of disappointment in yourself, or care about what you're supposed to be doing. But I don't have that. 

Like, my high school diploma is sitting on the third shelf of my bookcase, the one right next to the window. It's in this dark green padded folder with the school crest stamped on it in gold foil, and the gold is actually starting to flake off just a tiny bit on the left edge of the shield. I can see the little specks of gold dust on the wood of the shelf if the light hits it right. Sometimes my mom comes in to take my empty plates, and I see her look at that green folder, and then she looks at me just sitting on the bed. I know she's probably thinking about how I was supposed to be finishing that community college program by now. I just stopped going, you know. I didn't make a big decision to quit, I just stopped getting up to go. 

But when I look at the diploma, or when I think about the college classes I'm not taking, my chest doesn't get tight. I don't feel ashamed. I don't sit here thinking, "Oh, I'm so worthless, I'm a failure because I'm nineteen and I just watch the ceiling fan all day." I just look at the green folder. I look at the little flakes of gold on the wood. I don't feel bad about myself, and I don't feel good about myself either. 

I think a failure would be upset about failing. They would cry, or feel guilty that their mom is bringing them turkey sandwiches with the crusts cut off while they do absolutely nothing. But I don't feel guilty. It's just like the dust motes and the warped fan blade. I just exist in the room. There's no judgment attached to it in my head. I'm not worth less, I'm not worth more. I'm just... here. So, no, I haven't been feeling worthless.
Have you had any thoughts that you would be better off dead or thoughts of hurting yourself?

Um, dead? No. I don't... I don't think about that. Hurting myself... no. 

There is this pair of scissors on the desk in the corner of my room. They have these bright orange plastic handles, the kind they used to give us in middle school art class. The metal is a little dull on one side, and there is a tiny spot of dried white glue near the hinge from when I tried to fix a broken picture frame maybe three years ago. Sometimes the light from the streetlamp outside catches the metal at night, and it just shines there in the dark. I know people who are really sad, people who want to die, they might look at something sharp like that and think about using it to stop feeling so bad. They want the pain to end. But I don't have any pain to end. I just look at the scissors and think about how the orange plastic is slightly faded on the left grip. I don't want to pick them up. I don't want to hurt myself. 

I don't want to die, either. Dying seems like it would take a lot of effort, actually. You have to actively want something to change to want to be dead, I think. You have to be running away from something terrible. But I am not running. I am just sitting here. Breathing in and out. The air in my room always smells a little bit like the lavender laundry detergent my mom uses because she washes the curtains every single month, trying to keep the dust down since I am in here all the time. I just breathe it in. I don't wish I would stop breathing. It is just an automatic thing my body does, like my stomach growling when lunch is late. 

So, no, I haven't had any thoughts about being better off dead or hurting myself. I don't really have thoughts about being better off at all. I am just existing. It is just neutral.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you felt clearly depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

Um... you're asking me that again. The two weeks thing. I'm pretty sure we started with that exact question, didn't we? About feeling clearly depressed or down nearly every day. I don't know if you lost your place on your notepad, or if you're supposed to ask it twice just to see if I change my mind, but my answer hasn't changed. It's still no. I haven't had a two-week period like that. 

I don't really have periods of time that feel different from other periods of time anyway. Like, yesterday felt exactly the same as today, and last Tuesday felt exactly the same as yesterday. It all just blends together into one long stretch of sitting on my bed. There's this one spot on my bedspread where the quilt is wearing thin because I always sit in the exact same position, and the fabric is this faded blue color, but right where my left heel rests, the blue is almost completely white now. You can see the little individual threads pulling apart if you look really closely at it. I was looking at that spot for a long time this morning before my mom drove me to this appointment. Just looking at the white threads crossing over each other, making these tiny little squares of empty space where the blue used to be. 

I wasn't sad about the quilt wearing out, and I wasn't depressed or down about sitting there looking at it. I was just looking at it. So, even if you ask me a third time, or a fourth time, it's just going to be the same answer. Just no.
Over the past two years, have you ever had a depressed or low mood most of the day nearly every day?

I mean... now you're just stretching the time out. First it was two weeks, now it's two years. But changing the number of days doesn't change what I'm telling you. It's still no. I don't have a low mood. 

Actually, it's funny you say two years, because there is a calendar on the back of my bedroom door that is exactly two years old. It's from 2022. It has pictures of different national parks, and January is Yosemite. The picture has this huge, sheer gray rock face, and at the very bottom, there are these dark green pine trees with tiny patches of white snow on the branches. The bottom left corner of the paper is curled up into a little tube because the door brushes against the carpet whenever it opens, which isn't very often. I never flipped the page to February. It's just been stuck on January for two whole years. 

I look at that gray rock a lot. I've counted the pine trees. There are forty-seven of them, if you include the ones that are cut off by the edge of the glossy paper. And over the past two years, while that calendar has just been hanging there getting older, I've just been sitting here. The sun comes through the window, it makes a bright yellow rectangle on the carpet, the rectangle slowly stretches and moves across the floor toward the closet, and then it fades out and gets dark. That has happened over seven hundred times since that calendar was supposed to be used. 

And during all those days, I haven't felt low. I haven't felt depressed. I don't feel sad that I haven't changed the month or that I've just been watching the light move across the floor. It's just paper hanging on a door, and I'm just a person sitting on a bed. The time just passes. There's no mood attached to it at all, definitely not a depressed one. So, no, not over the past two years either.
Have you ever had a period of at least two weeks when you lost interest or pleasure in things nearly every day?

Well, I guess... I don't know if "lost interest" is the right way to put it. It's more like... I just can't make myself do anything anymore. Like, anything at all. It's not that I actively think, "Oh, I don't want to do this," it's just that the energy to start doing it isn't there. It's completely gone. 

Like, I used to knit. I have this whole plastic bin under my bed, it's one of those clear storage tubs with the snap-on blue lids, and it's completely full of yarn. There's this one skein of wool that's this really beautiful heather gray, and I bought it specifically to make a scarf for my mom for Christmas. I even bought the special wooden needles for it, the bamboo ones that make that soft clicking sound instead of the sharp metal sound when you work the stitches. But the yarn is still just sitting in the plastic bag from the craft store, right on top of the bin. I haven't touched it. I haven't even taken it out to feel how soft it is. 

I also used to keep a journal. It's a black Moleskine notebook, the kind with the little elastic band that holds it shut, and a ribbon bookmark that's frayed at the very end. It's sitting on my desk right next to those scissors I told you about. The last entry is from months ago. I just stopped writing. And I used to go for walks around the neighborhood, usually around 4:00 PM when the sun starts getting a little lower and the shadows get really long across the sidewalks, but I don't do that either. 

Now, I mostly just sit in my room. I sit on that same spot on the bed with the worn-out blue threads. I don't even change my clothes most days. I'm wearing the same gray sweatpants and this oversized black t-shirt that I've had on since... I don't even know, maybe Tuesday? The shirt has a tiny hole right near the collarbone on the left side, just big enough to fit the tip of a pencil through. I just sit there in these clothes, doing nothing. 

And my mom, she comes in sometimes, usually carrying laundry or a glass of water, and she'll stand there in the doorway with this worried look on her face. Her eyebrows get all pinched together in the middle, making these two deep vertical lines right above her nose, and she asks me what's wrong. She asks if I'm okay, if I need anything. And I just look at her. I look at those two lines between her eyebrows, and I realize that I barely even have the energy to open my mouth and answer her. It feels like my jaw weighs a hundred pounds. So I just kind of shrug, or mumble something that doesn't really mean anything, just so she'll stop asking. So, yeah, it's been way more than two weeks of that. Just... not doing anything. Not having the energy for anything.
Have you ever had a similar two-week period like this before in your life?

Um... no. I don't think so. Not before this. 

Because, like I was saying, I used to do things. I didn't just sit. When I was in high school, which wasn't even that long ago since I'm only nineteen, I never had a time where I just stayed in bed for weeks. I went to school every day. I had this locker on the second floor of the C building, locker number 412. It was painted this dull, rusty red color, but the paint was completely chipped away all around the combination dial, so you could see the shiny silver metal underneath it. And I used to walk up these three flights of stairs to get to it every single morning. 

The stairs had those black rubber treads on the edge of each step, and the tread on the middle stair of the second flight was peeling off on the left side, curled up just like that calendar page I told you about. So I always made sure to step on the far right side of that specific stair so I wouldn't trip. I did that every day at exactly 7:42 AM. And I carried this heavy navy blue backpack. The front zipper was stuck on a frayed piece of the inner nylon lining, so I had to leave that pocket half open all year. The backpack was really heavy because of my history and biology textbooks, but it wasn't heavy the way my arms and my jaw feel heavy now. It was just... normal heavy. Physical heavy. I had the energy to carry it up all those stairs. 

I didn't have any weeks where I couldn't do that. Even when we had winter break, which was exactly two weeks long, I didn't just sit around doing nothing. I would organize things in my room. I had this collection of little glass animal figurines on my windowsill, and I would take them all down, one by one, and dust them with a yellow microfiber cloth. I would line them up by height. There was a glass penguin with a tiny orange painted beak, and a glass elephant with its trunk pointing straight up in the air. I had the energy to do all of that. I actually wanted to do it. 

So, no. I've never had a time like this before. It's just been this one, long, continuous stretch now. Before this started, I was just doing normal things. I don't remember ever feeling this... empty of energy before in my life.
Before these last two years, was there ever a time when you felt depressed or down for at least two weeks?

I mean, like I said earlier about the calendar and everything, I haven't felt depressed or down recently, and I definitely didn't feel that way before all this started, either. I was just... normal. I wasn't sad. Like, back when I was going to high school and walking up those stairs to my locker, I wasn't walking around feeling low. 

After I put my heavy backpack in locker 412, I would go to my homeroom, which was room 204. Mr. Harrison's room. He had this massive poster of the periodic table on the back wall, but the element Bromine was completely faded to a pale yellow because the sun hit exactly that one square every morning at 8:15. I would sit in the third row, second desk from the door, and the desk had this deep scratch carved into the faux-wood laminate top that looked exactly like a lightning bolt. I used to trace it with the tip of my mechanical pencil, the clear plastic kind with the blue rubber grip that gets all squishy and sticky if you hold it too long. 

I would just sit there, tracing that lightning bolt, listening to the morning announcements come through that staticky gray speaker on the ceiling. I wasn't sad while I was doing that. I didn't feel down or depressed. I was just listening to the principal read the lunch menu. Usually it was pizza on Fridays, the rectangular kind with the tiny cubed pepperonis that curled up into little greasy bowls when they baked it. I didn't feel bad about the pizza, I didn't feel bad about the desk, I didn't feel bad about anything. I was just there. 

Even on the weekends, I would just sit on the front porch. We have these two green plastic Adirondack chairs, and the left one has a crack down the middle of the right armrest. I would sit in the one without the crack and watch the cars drive by on our street. I would count the silver ones. I didn't feel down then, either. I was just watching the tires spin. So, no, there was never a time where I felt depressed for two weeks before this. I just existed, doing regular things, tracing scratches and counting cars. There was no sadness in any of it.
How has your sleep been over these past two years—are you sleeping more, less, or about the same as usual?

I mean... I don't really think it's changed. It's just about the same, I guess. I haven't really noticed it being any different, mostly because I'm just in the room all the time anyway. 

Like I told you, I spend most of my time just sitting on that one spot on the bed. The quilt has this pattern of little white stars stitched into it, but right where I sit, three of the stars have completely lost their thread, so you can only see the faint little needle-holes showing where the shape used to be. When it gets dark, the light from the streetlamp outside comes through the window blinds and casts these long, perfectly straight yellow lines across the floor and up the side of the bed. Well, I guess... I don't know if "lost interest" is the right way to put it. It's more like... I just can't make myself do anything anymore. Like, anything at all. I even bought the special wooden needles for it, the bamboo ones that make that soft clicking sound instead of the sharp metal sound when you work the stitches. But the yarn is still just sitting in the plastic bag from the craft store, right on top of the bin. I haven't touched it. I haven't even taken it out to feel how soft it is. 

I also used to keep a journal. It's a black Moleskine notebook, the kind with the little elastic band that holds it shut, and a ribbon bookmark that's frayed at the very end. It's sitting on my desk right next to those scissors I told you about. The last entry is from months ago. I just stopped writing. And I used to go for walks around the neighborhood, usually around 4:00 PM when the sun starts getting a little lower and the shadows get really long across the sidewalks, but I don't do that either. 

Now, I mostly just sit in my room. I sit on that same spot on the bed with the worn-out blue threads. I don't even change my clothes most days. I'm wearing the same gray sweatpants and this oversized black t-shirt that I've had on since... I don't even know, maybe Tuesday? The shirt has a tiny hole right near the collarbone on the left side, just big enough to fit the tip of a pencil through. I just sit there in these clothes, doing nothing. 

And my mom, she comes in sometimes, usually carrying laundry or a glass of water, and she'll stand there in the doorway with this worried look on her face. Her eyebrows get all pinched together in the middle, making these two deep vertical lines right above her nose, and she asks me what's wrong. She asks if I'm okay, if I need anything. And I just look at her. I look at those two lines between her eyebrows, and I realize that I barely even have the energy to open my mouth and answer her. It feels like my jaw weighs a hundred pounds. So I just kind of shrug, or mumble something that doesn't really mean anything, just so she'll stop asking. So, yeah, it's been way more than two weeks of that. Just... not doing anything. Not having the energy for anything.

Um... no. I don't think so. Not before this. 

Because, like I was saying, I used to do things. I didn't just sit. When I was in high school, which wasn't even that long ago since I'm only nineteen, I never had a time where I just stayed in bed for weeks. I went to school every day. I had this locker on the second floor of the C building, locker number 412. It was painted this dull, rusty red color, but the paint was completely chipped away all around the combination dial, so you could see the shiny silver metal underneath it. And I used to walk up these three flights of stairs to get to it every single morning. 

The stairs had those black rubber treads on the edge of each step, and the tread on the middle stair of the second flight was peeling off on the left side, curled up just like that calendar page I told you about. So I always made sure to step on the far right side of that specific stair so I wouldn't trip. I did that every day at exactly 7:42 AM. And I carried this heavy navy blue backpack. The front zipper was stuck on a frayed piece of the inner nylon lining, so I had to leave that pocket half open all year. The backpack was really heavy because of my history and biology textbooks, but it wasn't heavy the way my arms and my jaw feel heavy now. It was just... normal heavy. Physical heavy. I had the energy to carry it up all those stairs. 

I didn't have any weeks where I couldn't do that. Even when we had winter break, which was exactly two weeks long, I didn't just sit around doing nothing. I would organize things in my room. I had this collection of little glass animal figurines on my windowsill, and I would take them all down, one by one, and dust them with a yellow microfiber cloth. I would line them up by height. There was a glass penguin with a tiny orange painted beak, and a glass elephant with its trunk pointing straight up in the air. I had the energy to do all of that. I actually wanted to do it. 

So, no. I've never had a time like this before. It's just been this one, long, continuous stretch now. Before this started, I was just doing normal things. I don't remember ever feeling this... empty of energy before in my life.

He had this massive poster of the periodic table on the back wall, but the element Bromine was completely faded to a pale yellow because the sun hit exactly that one square every morning at 8:15. I would sit in the third row, second desk from the door, and the desk had this deep scratch carved into the faux-wood laminate top that looked exactly like a lightning bolt. I can see the red light hitting the condensation on the side of the glass, and sometimes a water drop gets too heavy and slides all the way down to the bottom, making a little puddle on the fake wood of the nightstand. I just watch the red light on the water drops until I fall asleep. And then I wake up, and the red numbers are different—maybe it says 8:14 instead of 11:32—but the room feels exactly the same. The blinking dots just keep going. So I'm not sleeping for days at a time, and I'm not staying awake all night, either. I remember sitting in the student union building on that first day, just looking at that map. The chairs in there were covered in this scratchy maroon fabric, the kind that catches on the back of your jeans when you shift your weight, and the carpet was this ugly mix of brown and gray squares.
